findings.title: Google refresh stores Zod SafeParse wrapper as credential key
findings.body: In GoogleCalendarService refreshAccessToken, `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` returns a SafeParse result `{ success, data, error }`, not the parsed tokens. The code then does `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, persisting the wrapper object as the credential key. The previous code used `googleCredentialSchema.parse()` which returns the data directly. After one refresh every Google credential becomes `{success:true,data:{...}}` and subsequent `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` will fail or produce wrong credentials, breaking Google Calendar sync.

findings.title: Dummy refresh_token overwrites real refresh token
findings.body: parseRefreshTokenResponse does `if (!data.refresh_token) data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. When credential-sync is enabled the external endpoint intentionally returns only access_token+expiry with no refresh_token. The literal string "refresh_token" is then merged/spread into the credential and persisted (e.g. Office365, Google, Zoom paths), permanently destroying the real refresh_token in the DB. Later non-synced refreshes will send the literal string as the refresh token and fail.

findings.title: Minimum token schema uses computed nonsense keys and strips tokens
findings.body: minimumTokenResponseSchema is declared with `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` as keys. Those expressions evaluate to a fixed string like the Zod type's toString output, not a wildcard/record. Zod objects strip unknown keys by default, so in sync mode the schema effectively keeps only `access_token` and drops `expiry_date`/`expires_in`/`refresh_token` etc. Callers that spread `tokenResponse.data` back into the credential therefore lose expiry data or must rely on the dummy placeholder, causing immediate re-refresh loops or invalid credentials.

findings.title: Sync path always returns fetch Response but callers expect other shapes
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens returns a `fetch` Response when syncing, otherwise returns whatever `refreshFunction()` returns. Google expects `fetchTokens.res` with `.data` (`const token = res?.data`), HubSpot expects a HubSpot token object directly, Zoho/Zoho-Bigin expect an axios response with `.data`. In sync mode Google gets `res.data === undefined` and crashes on `token.access_token`, HubSpot stores a Response object as tokens (expiresIn becomes NaN), Zoho/Bigin crash on `tokenInfo.data.error` because fetch Response has no `.data`. Only callers that already use fetch + handleErrorsJson keep working. The abstraction is type-incompatible.

findings.title: Salesforce service uses prisma without importing it
findings.body: SalesforceCalendarService.getClient calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)` but the file never imports `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma`. At runtime `prisma` is an undefined reference and every Salesforce calendar operation throws ReferenceError. This is a newly added code path that runs on every getClient call, so Salesforce integration is completely broken.

findings.title: Salesforce connection uses stale tokens after refresh
findings.body: getClient fetches new tokens into `accessTokenParsed.data` and persists them, but then constructs `new jsforce.Connection({ ... accessToken: credentialKey.access_token, refreshToken: credentialKey.refresh_token })` from the old `credentialKey` instead of the refreshed values. The current request therefore authenticates with the expired token that just triggered the refresh, so the refresh has no effect for this call and will be repeated on every call.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh failure check uses statusText instead of ok
findings.body: The new Salesforce refresh does `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw`. `statusText` is implementation-dependent and often empty with undici/node-fetch, and Salesforce can return non-OK bodies with 200 or OK text with errors. The correct check is `!response.ok`. As written the code can throw on successful refreshes or miss failed refreshes and then try to parse an error page as tokens.

findings.title: Bigin passes credentialId as calcomUserId to sync endpoint
findings.body: BiginCalendarService.refreshAccessToken takes `(credentialId, credentialKey)` and calls `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)`. The third parameter is documented as `userId` and other services pass `credential.userId`, and the sync endpoint receives it as `calcomUserId`. Bigin therefore sends the credential primary key where the remote expects a user id, so the remote will look up the wrong user or fail. It should pass the credential's userId, not the credential id.

findings.title: Credential webhook has no method check and unhandled parse/decrypt errors
findings.body: The handler accepts any HTTP method (including GET) to create/overwrite credentials, does `schema.parse(req.body)` without try/catch so invalid bodies throw 500 instead of 400, and does `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` without error handling. A wrong encryption key, corrupted payload, or non-JSON plaintext crashes the endpoint with 500 and can leak stack traces. It should restrict to POST, return 400 on validation/decryption failures, and not expose internal errors.

findings.title: Outbound credential-sync request sends no auth and ignores failures
findings.body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId`+`appSlug` as URLSearchParams with no Content-Type, no webhook secret, and no signature, so the self-hosted endpoint cannot authenticate that the request came from Cal.com. The code also never checks `response.ok` before returning, so 4xx/5xx HTML error pages are passed to token parsers and treated as token refresh failures, which can incorrectly mark credentials invalid.
